analysis.one_liner: Gives registered voters $100 in public vouchers to give to federal candidates.
analysis.headline: Gillibrand's public campaign financing bill drew zero cosponsors and has sat in the Senate Rules Committee with no action since its August 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a 'Democracy Dollars' program: any registered voter could request $100 in public vouchers and direct them to candidates for the House, Senate, or President. Candidates who join the program must give up large checks — individual contributions would be capped at $1,000 and step down to $200 by 2037 — and cannot spend more than $2,500 of their own money. The bill repeals the old presidential public financing tax checkoff and replaces it with this voucher system. It was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who don't write big campaign checks: the bill hands every eligible voter up to $100 per election to spend on candidates, funded by taxpayers, and creates an outreach program specifically aimed at people who have never contributed to a campaign. It also helps candidates who lack access to wealthy donor networks, since they can qualify for the program by raising $50,000 (House), $500,000 (Senate), or $1,000,000 (President) in small amounts and vouchers.

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible registered voter can request Democracy Dollars — $100 for each House, Senate, and presidential election, primary and general — and transfer them in $10 increments to participating candidates of their choice, with public money paid into the candidate's account.

Participating candidates must rely on small donations: individual contributions are capped at $1,000 starting in 2029 and step down every two years to $200 by 2037, and candidates cannot spend more than $2,500 of their own or immediate family's money.

The Federal Election Commission must run an outreach program targeting communities and individuals who have not previously made political contributions, and a pilot program for mailing vouchers to expand participation.

The bill's voucher amounts automatically increase if candidates outside the program continue to raise more money on average than participating candidates, so small-dollar candidates are not left behind as campaign costs rise.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers pay for the vouchers through an open-ended appropriation — 'such sums as necessary' with no dollar cap in the bill. Wealthy donors and bundlers lose their privileged channel into participating candidates' campaigns, as contributions are capped and eventually limited to $200. Taxpayers also lose the option of the old $3 presidential campaign checkoff, which the bill repeals.

drawbacks.text: The funding is an uncapped, open-ended appropriation: if a large share of the roughly 200 million-plus eligible voters used their full allotment across primaries and general elections, the cost would run into the tens of billions of dollars per election cycle.

The bill does nothing about independent expenditures: super PACs and outside groups could still spend unlimited money to shape the same elections, so large donors would keep an avenue to influence races even while candidate financing is public.

Participating candidates' contribution cap drops to $200 by 2037, which could leave them badly outspent by non-participating rivals unless the automatic increase in voucher amounts keeps pace — a risk the bill acknowledges by requiring the FEC to review whether participants can 'compete.'

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: taxpayers fund a per-voucher system that dilutes the power of large donors and gives every voter real spending power in elections. The cost is real but bounded per voter ($100 per election per office), though the overall program price is left to uptake. The honest weakness is the bill's silence on outside spending — it reforms the money that flows through candidates but not the super PAC money that flows around them, so its effect on who wins elections would depend partly on whether candidates stay in the program.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate in August 2026 and sent to the Rules and Administration Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the Clean Elections Act on August 6, 2026; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been recorded since the referral.
The 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027, leaving roughly five months for the bill to advance from committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved and no one has been blocked; the practical beneficiaries of the status quo are incumbents' existing fundraising networks and large donors, who keep the current system intact as long as the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors and incumbents' fundraising networks

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — no hearing or markup scheduled
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on August 6, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no positions beyond the sponsor's are on the record; the absence of any cosponsors is the only signal available.

industries.note: Participating candidates can accept only small individual contributions, stepping down to $200 by 2037, eliminating the six- and seven-figure check that gives wealthy donors outsized access. Vouchers give ordinary voters countervailing spending power.
The bill regulates money flowing through candidates but leaves outside spending untouched, effectively locking super PACs in as the remaining channel for large money to influence the same elections.

Publicly funded vouchers become campaign spending that flows to media buys and consultants, expanding the pool of money candidates can spend — though the firms' role is unchanged from the current system.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action five months after introduction, and the session ending January 3, 2027, the bill has no visible path to a vote. It will almost certainly expire at the end of the 119th Congress unless reintroduced in the next one.
